transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-04-07 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Recording: Fireflies export
- Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (SE), Luis (SE Console), Evan (CTO OpenBridge), Sara (Lead ML), Markus (Platform), Nadia (Security)

Summary: quick migration/parity demo focused on switching endpoints from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood API. Showed parity mapping approach, console routing, and Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization. Customer expressed constraints around SOC2 + KMS + VPC/private deployment and tight latency SLOs on their conversational product.

Topics covered: parity mapping table, cost vs latency tradeoffs, dedicated vs hosted, private/VPC options, KV cache & prefix caching, batching strategies, quantization compatibility, SSO and audit logs. Links referenced: Deck - https://redwood.ai/decks/openbridge-parity-2026, Parity sheet - drive.openbridge/parity-sample (placeholder), Benchmark spreadsheet: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/obg-sample

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm jordan from redwood, i'm the AE on this account. quick intros?
[00:04] Evan: yep Evan here, CTO at OpenBridge. we run the conversation platform — latency is, like, everything.
[00:08] Sara: Sara, lead ML engineer. mostly responsible for model endpoints and runtime.
[00:11] Markus: Markus, infra — networking and security.
[00:14] Nadia: Nadia, security architect, we need SOC2 and kms gating for customer data.
[00:18] Jordan: great, thanks. priya and luis from our side will walk through parity mapping and console bits. we want to show how you can route requests from your current openai/anthropic/together mix into redwood with the same inputs and nearly identical outputs and explain the ops side.
[00:30] Priya: hi all — i'll start with the high level parity approach. we do a model mapping table — for each external model you call we pick a Redwood-verified variant, and then tune prompt templates, temperature, max tokens to match behavior. small caveat: some models need small prompt engineering changes because tokenization differs.
[00:46] Sara: tokenization differences — that is our main worry; we have a lot of prompt-engineered chains where token offsets matter.
[00:51] Priya: totally. we usually recommend adding a lightweight validation layer: run n responses on both sides and diff output distributions. we'll supply a small harness.
[01:02] Luis: i'll jump into the console — here's the route we created for your 'chat' endpoint. (screen share) you can see routing rules: primary hosted redwood model, fallback to a cheaper quantized variant, and a regional fallback.
[01:15] Markus: when you say fallback — is that automatic? will it change the output format?
[01:18] Priya: automatic based on policy you configure. format stays consistent if the model variant supports tool-calling / streaming. we preserve the same response envelope so your parser shouldn't break in most cases.
[01:29] Evan: what's the latency difference between the hosted and the quantized fallback?
[01:32] Priya: depends on seq length and model family; we saw 10-30% slower generation on aggressive quantization for some workloads, but 2-3x cost reduction. for short-turn conversational loads with low token per request, often the delta is smaller.
[01:46] Sara: how about KV cache — we heavily rely on a prefix cache for few-shot prompts to avoid recomputation.
[01:51] Priya: Redwood supports prefix/KV caching across variants. caching reduces token compute cost and latency. note that cache keys are deterministic based on prompt and model variant so if you change model variant keys change — we've got tools to migrate caches or keep a shared cache namespace.
[02:07] Jordan: quick interjection — i want to address the security questions up front. Nadia, you mentioned SOC2 and KMS. we have SOC2 Type II (link in the deck) and support customer-managed KMS for Private deployments; hosted can use redwood-managed keys with strict isolation.
[02:24] Nadia: do you have auditable request logs and token redaction? we need tamper-evident logs and a way to show PII was redacted.
[02:32] Luis: yes, audit logs with immutability windows and optional redaction are in the console. logs can be pushed to your SIEM or to an S3 bucket in your VPC.
[02:40] Nadia: ok, can we see an example?
[02:42] Luis: (shares example) here's a sample audit record. note the fields: request id, model, tokens consumed, user id, and a redaction flag; we also support HSM-backed signatures for log entries on Private.
[02:58] Evan: great. let's talk about migrations steps — we have three endpoints: one for short chat, one for long-form summarization (higher token counts), and a reranker. can we keep the same API paths?
[03:08] Priya: yes — two options: 1) adapter layer in your infra that translates openai/anthropic calls to Redwood API with minimal changes; or 2) use our console routing to accept the same external path and do in-platform mapping. most customers do a hybrid: adapter for immediate cutover and console routing for long-term ops.
[03:26] Sara: for the reranker we use embeddings + cosine — are embeddings compatible?
[03:30] Priya: our embedding models produce embeddings in the same vector space conventions; cosine/similarity works. we include scaling guidance since different tokenizers can change average vector norms slightly. we'll give a script to normalize vectors for parity.
[03:45] Markus: network — if we go Private, what are the egress requirements and does Redwood need inbound connectivity?
[03:51] Luis: Private can be deployed in your VPC with no public inbound. we can provide a customer-managed control plane and a data plane in your subnets; egress to our control plane is optional depending on on-prem vs private cloud. we'll send a network runbook.
[04:05] Nadia: SLA and data residency?
[04:08] Jordan: Dedicated/reserved gives SLA-backed latency and uptime, Private gives you control on residency. hosted is multi-region and we have region pinning. SLA details in the pricing sheet.
[04:18] Evan: cost — show me an apples-to-apples example for our current mix: 60% chat short (avg 40 tokens), 30% reranker (embeddings heavy), 10% long summarization (avg 1200 tokens).
[04:30] Jordan: right, we prepared a parity cost example in the deck. (shares) overall for your profile, initial numbers show ~25-40% cost reduction if you adopt batching + caching + a mix of quantized variants for non-prod. production critical chat we usually keep on a higher-fidelity hosted variant or Dedicated.
[04:48] Sara: can you explain the batching recommendations — we can't introduce tail latency on chat.
[04:53] Priya: batching is workload-aware; we have continuous batching and we also support a latency SLO knob. for high priority chat you can set small max batch windows, or pin to Dedicated instances to avoid queuing. costs rise with lower latency but SLOs are kept.
[05:10] Markus: curious — you mentioned KV cache migration earlier. if we change model family, will our cache invalidation cause cold starts?
[05:17] Priya: yes potentially. two approaches: keep parallel caches and warm them during a staged rollout; or run a deterministic migration job that re-encodes keys into the new variant namespace. we can provide tooling for both.
[05:29] Evan: walk us through an actual parity mapping for a TogetherAI model we use (together/xglm-large-ish) to a Redwood variant.
[05:36] Priya: sure. in the parity sheet we mapped together/xglm-large to redwood/titan-large-compat (example). adjustments: lower temperature by 0.05 and add a small instruction token at the start to compensate for tokenizer differences. we ran 500 prompts and saw 92% semantic parity and BLEU-like metrics within acceptable bounds.
[05:58] Sara: 92% — what's the failure mode on the 8%? hallucination or formatting?
[06:02] Priya: mostly formatting differences and rare factual cutoff differences. that's why we recommend running you own evals. we'll help you set up regression alerts in Redwood Optimize bound to your prompt sets.
[06:16] Jordan: Luis — show the Optimize suggestions panel and rule set for cost/perf tradeoffs.
[06:20] Luis: (screen) here's Optimize — it surfaced a suggestion to enable prefix caching for the chat route and to lower the batching window for high-priority paths. it also suggested a quantization profile for non-prod. you can accept suggestions and auto-apply to a canary group.
[06:36] Markus: can we run canaries per-user segment? we need to test only a small subset of tenant IDs.
[06:40] Luis: yes, route policies support attribute-based targeting — user id, tenant id, or request headers. canarying is built-in.
[06:46] Nadia: about keys — customer-managed KMS: do you rotate keys? and what about log encryption?
[06:52] Priya: keys rotate per your schedule for Private; for hosted we manage rotation but rotations are logged. logs can be encrypted with your KMS if using Private and the data plane in your VPC.
[07:04] Evan: ok nice. let's talk about the demo steps — are you able to show a live run of a conversion from an OpenAI API call to Redwood?
[07:11] Jordan: yes, priya will trigger a simple adapter demo. note: small audio lag sharing.
[07:16] Priya: (runs script) here's an example request using openai chat completions schema, we proxy it through the adapter and hit Redwood's chat route. (timestamped response shows) you can see the JSON envelope is identical — only the authorization header changed and we add a stub header redwood-model.
[07:32] Sara: i see streaming — works fine. output looks similar. did you map token limit differences?
[07:36] Priya: mapped via the adapter: we enforce the min(max_tokens, model_limit) and send warnings if truncation occurs.
[07:45] Markus: for embeddings — how do we validate parity numerically?
[07:49] Priya: we'll provide a small colab/harness to compute cosine similarities and a threshold table. also suggest running an AB test on downstream ranking to detect regressions.
[07:58] Jordan: quick Q for Evan — what's your timeline and must-have success criteria?
[08:02] Evan: timeline: pilot in 3–4 weeks, production in Q3 if pilot good. success: <5% user-visible regressions, <10% cost reduction target, and security sign-off.
[08:12] Jordan: good — we'll tailor the pilot to that.
[08:15] Sara: edge-case question: we sometimes use function-calling / tool-calls; does Redwood support the same structured tool calling semantics?
[08:22] Priya: yes, we support structured outputs and function-calling. minor differences in type coercions sometimes appear so we recommend a small wrapper to validate schemas.
[08:33] Luis: also note streaming and chunked tool-calls are supported; we also surface per-token costs in console.
[08:40] Nadia: do you store full request payloads in hosted? we need retention controls and deletion on demand.
[08:46] Jordan: retention policies are configurable. hosted has retention tiers; Dedicated and Private give you tighter control and deletion APIs. we'll include the retention matrix.
[08:58] Evan: can you run a cost estimate if we opt for Dedicated for chat but hosted for embedding?
[09:03] Jordan: yes — we can model hybrid: Dedicated pool for low-latency chat, hosted fallback for long-running summarization and embedding workloads. the parity sheet has a hybrid tab and example numbers.
[09:13] Sara: what about training vs inference differences — not a training scenario for us, but does Redwood's runtime require any model conversion?
[09:19] Priya: we handle model variants during onboarding; for open models we validate compatibility and, if needed, produce an optimized quantized artifact. we don't retrain models — just compile and optimize for inference.
[09:28] Markus: can the control plane be run on-prem?
[09:31] Luis: yes — for the Private option we can provide a customer-managed control plane. some customers prefer a hybrid where telemetry goes to a control plane in our cloud but data plane runs in their VPC.
[09:43] Evan: ok can we talk about a short pilot plan? what do you need from us to spin up a pilot next week?
[09:49] Jordan: minimum: sample traffic logs, a set of representative prompts and example user ids, network details for Private pilot or API keys for hosted pilot. priya will send the harness.
[09:58] Priya: i'll include a short list of 20–30 prompts per endpoint and a script to run parity tests and collect metrics: latency, token counts, semantic similarity, and fail rates.
[10:08] Nadia: i want to see the SOC2 plus encryption details before we sign any NDA addendum.
[10:12] Jordan: understood — we'll share the security pack and propose a security deep dive with our security team.
[10:18] Evan: cool. any blockers you foresee?
[10:21] Priya: mainly cache migration and tokenizer differences for edge cases — both solvable with the harness and a staged rollout.
[10:27] Sara: one more — we have a reranking latency SLO at 100ms p95; will Redwood meet that with embeddings pipeline?
[10:33] Priya: embeddings are compute heavy but with a Dedicated pool and proper batching we typically hit that range; for 100ms p95 you might need co-located index/ANN nearest neighbor infra; we can help size.
[10:45] Markus: add to action items: we'll share a perf histogram for reranker.
[10:49] Jordan: perfect. quick recap of next steps: we'll share parity spreadsheet + repo, priya will provide harness, security docs go to Nadia, and we'll schedule the security deep dive for 4/14.
[11:02] Evan: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[11:05] Jordan: thanks — end meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: speaker labels occasionally generic, small transcription errors present (e.g., together -> to gather, KV -> K V, some punctuation missing).

Attachments referenced: parity deck (https://redwood.ai/decks/openbridge-parity-2026), parity mapping CSV (drive.openbridge/parity-sample), benchmark script repo (https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/tree/openbridge), security pack (link in follow-up email).
